strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored computer-vision problem: spatially grounded language generation from whole-body 3D PET/CT. Combining PET, CT, and lesion masks is clinically motivated, and the proposed focal crop is a sensible response to lesions occupying less than 1% of a scan.

PETAR-11K is potentially valuable: 11,356 lesion descriptions from 5,126 examinations, multiple radiotracers, and paired volumetric images, masks, and text would constitute a meaningful resource if its annotations and release are adequately validated.

The evaluation covers 2D, 3D, and mask-aware models and uses lexical, semantic, and clinically oriented metrics. Fine-tuned M3D-RAD and Reg2RG comparisons are more informative than zero-shot comparisons alone.

PETAR substantially outperforms the fine-tuned baselines in Table 3, including M3D-RAD on ROUGE-L (0.519 vs. 0.446), BERTScore (0.791 vs. 0.750), RaTEScore (0.708 vs. 0.627), and GREEN (0.246 vs. 0.071).

The attempt to measure correlations between automated metrics and physician judgments is useful; the reported result that GREEN correlates best with human scores could inform evaluation of future PET reporting systems.
weaknesses: The central clinical claims are not supported by the reported human evaluation. The manuscript describes a second study in which five nuclear-medicine physicians rated correctness, localization, and clinical utility, but reports none of those ratings, baseline comparisons, uncertainty, or inter-rater agreement. Table 5 only correlates metrics with scores from a separate 100-pair study. Consequently, the conclusion that human evaluation demonstrates accurate and clinically useful findings is unsubstantiated.

The automatically constructed dataset receives no annotation-quality evaluation. There is no manual audit of sentence filtering, SUV/slice extraction, lesion-component matching, anatomical fields produced by Qwen, or threshold-derived masks. Matching a component using a report-derived SUV within ±0.1 and one axial slice can select physiological uptake or the wrong lesion. Since dataset validity underlies both training and testing, this is a material technical weakness.

The data partition is not specified. The paper gives the benchmark size but not train/validation sizes or whether splitting is disjoint by lesion, examination, patient, longitudinal series, or institution. Multiple lesions occur within examinations and patients may have repeated scans, so leakage could substantially inflate language and anatomy metrics.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently documented. The manuscript does not explain how volumetric studies and masks are converted for 2D models, which slices are selected, whether prompts and decoding are standardized, or provide complete fine-tuning recipes. Comparing PETAR trained through four stages with mostly non-fine-tuned models is not persuasive; even the selected fine-tuned baselines lack enough detail to establish matched optimization and compute.

The ablation evidence does not support several stated conclusions. Relative to the TotalSegmentator-pretrained baseline, adding only the mask lowers BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore, and RaTEScore; adding only CT similarly lowers most metrics. The focal prompt accounts for nearly all of the improvement. The claim of sequentially consistent gains and strong individual contributions from mask and CT contradicts Table 4, and no factorial interaction analysis or uncertainty is provided.

The method is under-specified. MaskEmbed, focal crop size, handling of variable lesion sizes, PET/CT intensity normalization, token dimensions, pooling, and inference decoding are omitted. The equations add global and focal token sequences without explaining how their patch grids are aligned. The figure refers to convolutional layers while the text specifies patch embeddings. Training hyperparameters are deferred to supplementary material that is not present in the provided manuscript.

Several quantitative claims are inaccurate or overstated. The increase from 0.137 to 0.531 BLEU over InternVL3 is about 288% relative, not 29%. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests accompany the results. The two displayed PETAR examples also contain incorrect region/subsite, SUV, or slice information relative to ground truth, which conflicts with broad claims of factual accuracy.

The manuscript does not characterize cohort demographics, scanner/protocol variation, site composition, tracer counts, disease distribution, or inclusion criteria. This prevents assessment of generalization and bias. Evaluation appears to use the same automatically generated annotation pipeline as training, with no external-site or independently annotated test set.

Reproducibility and availability are currently weak: despite calling PETAR-11K publicly available and PETAR-Bench reproducible, the paper supplies no repository, dataset identifier, license, access procedure, code, or model weights. Ethical approval is mentioned, but privacy risks associated with releasing clinical text and volumes are not discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: grounded lesion-level description of volumetric PET/CT. Combining whole-volume PET/CT context with a high-resolution focal crop is sensible for lesions occupying less than 1% of the scan. The resulting model substantially outperforms the strongest fine-tuned baselines on the reported automated metrics.
The study considers diverse metric families and attempts expert evaluation rather than relying exclusively on lexical similarity.
The manuscript is generally easy to follow, and the qualitative examples make the intended lesion-captioning task concrete.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified to establish validity. The manuscript gives no train/validation/test split sizes or procedure, does not state whether splitting is performed at the patient level, and does not explain whether PETAR-Bench is independent of training data. With multiple lesions and potentially multiple exams per patient, leakage could materially inflate performance.

The automatically constructed supervision is not validated. Masks are selected by matching reported slice and SUVmax values, while an LLM ensemble extracts those values and Qwen rewrites the text into a structured schema. The paper reports no expert audit, extraction accuracy, mask quality, ambiguity/failure rate, or evidence that rewriting preserves the original findings. Errors in this pipeline affect both training labels and benchmark references.

The claimed human evidence is largely absent. Although two evaluations are described, the paper only reports correlations between metrics and average human scores. It provides no model-level physician ratings, confidence intervals, inter-rater agreement, statistical tests, blinding protocol, or direct comparison with baselines. The second evaluation is also very small and ambiguously described: each of five physicians assessed only 16 lesions from eight patients. Consequently, the conclusion that experts demonstrated clinical usefulness is unsupported.

The ablation results contradict the accompanying claims. Mask-only and CT-only variants generally perform worse than the TotalSegmentator baseline; adding CT to the focal configuration sharply reduces RaTEScore from 0.698 to 0.587; and the full model is not best on CIDEr, where CT plus focal input without explicit mask conditioning scores 0.428 versus 0.415. Thus, the reported evidence does not show consistent improvements or the claimed synergy.

The central mask-awareness claim is not cleanly isolated. Even rows marked as having no mask input apparently require the mask to define the focal crop, so lesion location is still supplied indirectly. The large improvement comes primarily from focal cropping, a previously used idea, whereas explicit mask embedding provides marginal or inconsistent benefit. No direct grounding or localization metric is reported.

Baseline fairness is unclear. PETAR is trained on the new dataset, whereas most 2D and 3D models appear to be evaluated without equivalent adaptation; only selected 'best' models are fine-tuned. The paper does not specify 2D slice selection, prompting, preprocessing, tuning budgets, or checkpoint selection. Results also lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates.

The paper overstates the scope as PET automated reporting. The evaluated task generates a description for a supplied positive-lesion mask; lesion detection, segmentation, negative findings, complete report assembly, and impression generation are outside the method. The authors themselves identify these components as future work.

The qualitative examples expose clinically important inaccuracies: PETAR changes SUVmax and slice values in both examples and introduces an unsupported tendinopathy interpretation in one. These errors conflict with claims of factual accuracy and clinical utility, yet no dedicated measurement-error or hallucination analysis is provided.

Technical and reproducibility details are incomplete. The focal crop size and resizing, mask embedding, intensity normalization, patch dimensions, token alignment between global and focal inputs, spatial pooling, optimizer settings, and inference configuration are absent. It is also unclear how global and focal token sequences can be added when their spatial dimensions differ. The manuscript refers to supplementary hyperparameters, but they are not present in the provided submission, and no code or data-access link is given.

Several quantitative statements are inaccurate or overstated. For example, BLEU rises from 0.137 to 0.531 relative to InternVL3, which is approximately a 288% relative increase, not 29%. The paper also calls the full configuration best overall despite the CIDEr counterexample. External-site evaluation, radiotracer-specific analysis, demographic information, and acquisition-distribution details are missing, leaving generalization unestablished. These combined concerns are material rather than presentation-only issues and outweigh the promising problem formulation and reported metric gains.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: grounded lesion-level finding generation from whole-body 3D PET/CT, where lesions are small and volumetric inputs are challenging.
The reported dataset is substantial for this domain, containing 11,356 lesion descriptions from 5,126 examinations with aligned PET, CT, and lesion masks across multiple radiotracers.

The focal-crop design is sensible for preserving information about lesions occupying less than 1% of a scan. The comparison with a dataset-finetuned M3D-RAD baseline provides evidence that PETAR's overall configuration improves generation quality, including GREEN from 0.071 to 0.246 and BERTScore from 0.750 to 0.791.

Evaluation covers lexical, semantic, and radiology-oriented metrics, and the metric-versus-expert correlation study is useful: GREEN has the strongest reported correlation with human judgment (Spearman rho=0.608).

The clinical motivation, dataset-construction pipeline, and intended workflow are generally understandable, and qualitative examples illustrate both the task and the differences from the strongest baseline.
weaknesses: The experimental split is not described. It is unclear whether separation is performed by lesion, examination, patient, or longitudinal patient history. Because multiple lesions can come from one examination and patients may have repeated scans, leakage could substantially inflate all reported results; this is a material validity and reproducibility concern.

The claimed human support is not actually reported. The manuscript describes two reader studies but provides no PETAR-versus-baseline human scores, uncertainty, significance tests, inter-rater agreement, or clear assignment protocol. The second study is also called larger despite reporting only 16 lesions per expert. Consequently, claims that experts establish clinical accuracy or utility are unsupported by the presented evidence.

The ablation does not substantiate several architectural claims. The focal prompt accounts for nearly all of the gain, whereas adding the mask sometimes reduces BLEU/CIDEr and provides only small gains on other metrics; adding CT without the focal prompt also degrades most scores. This conflicts with the stated consistent improvements and synergy. Tests with corrupted, shifted, absent, or independently predicted masks are needed to demonstrate genuine mask grounding rather than reliance on the crop.

Dataset labels and masks are automatically derived from report-provided SUV and slice information and then rewritten by an LLM, but their accuracy is not quantitatively validated against manual annotations. Evaluation against similarly processed text may reward schema/style matching, while threshold-derived masks may differ from masks produced by the proposed real-world upstream segmenters.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently documented. The manuscript does not specify how volumetric data and masks are converted for 2D models, what prompts and decoding settings are used, or why only selected baselines are finetuned. Thus, the broad claim of superiority over 2D and 3D VLMs is difficult to interpret, although the finetuned M3D-RAD comparison remains informative.

Important implementation details are missing from the provided manuscript, including train/validation/test sizes, crop resolution and size, mask embedding, spatial pooling, preprocessing/intensity normalization, optimization settings, and inference configuration. No code, dataset access mechanism, or benchmark release link is given despite claims of public availability and reproducibility.

Some quantitative and qualitative claims are overstated. For example, the increase from 0.137 to 0.531 BLEU is approximately 288%, not 29%, and the shown examples contain region mismatches and unsupported diagnostic interpretation. These issues are correctable, but they weaken confidence in the analysis and clinical framing.

strengths: PETARSeg-11K could be a valuable computer-vision resource: it links 11,356 lesion descriptions from 5,126 whole-body PET/CT exams to 3D masks, addressing a clinically relevant modality and grounding granularity that are poorly represented in existing datasets.

The combination of PET, CT, lesion localization, and a high-resolution focal crop is well motivated for lesions occupying less than 0.1% of a whole-body volume. PETAR-4B substantially improves every reported automatic metric over the strongest fine-tuned baselines, including GREEN from 0.086 to 0.257 and CIDEr from 0.132 to 0.457.
The evaluation includes diverse lexical, semantic, and clinical metrics, comparisons with both 2D and 3D models, component ablations, qualitative examples, and an external autoPET experiment.

The blinded evaluation by five board-certified nuclear-medicine physicians is a notable effort. Providing scoring rubrics and examining correlations between automatic metrics and expert judgments are useful contributions beyond benchmark performance.
The manuscript is generally clear, visually polished, and candidly identifies both the dependence on externally supplied masks and hallucination of quantitative measurements.
weaknesses: The data-splitting protocol is not reported. The paper states only that 1,175 "samples" are held out, although multiple lesions can come from the same exam and potentially the same patient/report. Unless splitting is performed at least by patient, nearly identical volumes and correlated report language can occur in training and test sets. This is a consequential leakage risk that undermines all internal results.

The ablation evidence does not support several central claims. The focal-only row already obtains nearly all of the gain, while explicit mask conditioning adds little or sometimes reduces metrics: adding the mask to the focal model changes CIDEr from 0.397 to 0.381 and BLEU from 0.528 to 0.525. Likewise, CT does not consistently help. Moreover, a "focal but no mask" configuration still uses the mask to define the crop, so it is not genuinely mask-agnostic. The claim that every component improves all metrics is directly contradicted by Table 3.

Baseline comparisons confound architecture with input and resolution. PETAR receives PET, CT, a mask-derived focal crop, and explicit mask features, whereas the principal 3D baseline uses global volume encoding; the 2D baselines receive only three PET slices. A baseline given the same PET/CT focal crop, or an otherwise matched crop-and-fusion architecture without the proposed conditioning, is needed to attribute gains to PETAR rather than privileged localized input.

The human study omits clinically important numerical errors even though the manuscript explicitly reports hallucinated SUV, size, and slice values. Replacing all numbers with [#] makes the reported utility scores inapplicable to the model's actual output, and the proposed deterministic replacement procedure is not implemented or evaluated. PETAR is strictly preferred in only 15/116 cases, versus 47/116 for the original report; grouping 54 ties with wins to claim approximately 60% preference is overly favorable.

The reader-study analysis lacks uncertainty estimates, significance tests, inter-reader agreement, and a clear account of whether scores are averaged per case or pooled across readers. No competing model is included in this study, so it does not validate the claimed clinical superiority over baselines. Correlations computed from a small, dependent set of ratings are likewise reported without confidence intervals.

The external evaluation is only 32 manually curated autoPET cases, has no reference text or baseline comparisons, and its selection procedure is unspecified. It therefore provides limited evidence for the claim of consistent out-of-distribution performance, especially given the single-center, older-scanner training cohort.

The benchmark masks are constructed using SUVmax and slice information extracted from the target reports. This creates a report-derived localization benchmark rather than an end-to-end automated-reporting setting. The system neither detects findings nor generates a complete report, and it does not assess missed lesions or negative findings; the broader automated-reporting and clinical-workflow claims are consequently overstated.

Dataset quality and availability are insufficiently documented. The cited 98% contour-location accuracy from prior work does not establish the accuracy of all 11,356 masks, lesion-text correspondences, or Qwen-generated structured fields. The manuscript gives no validation sample size, extraction-error analysis, release link, license, or concrete access procedure despite repeatedly calling the dataset publicly available.

Important implementation details are missing or inconsistent: the variable-sized focal tokens cannot be added to global tokens as written without an unreported resizing/alignment step; crop size, patch size, intensity preprocessing, inference-time cropping, and train/validation counts are absent; and the main text says each stage uses 10 epochs while the supplement lists 5. These issues materially limit reproducibility.

The architectural originality is moderate: the main effective idea is a 3D adaptation of previously proposed focal prompting combined with established mask conditioning and an M3D/Phi-3 backbone. The potentially high-value dataset could justify this incremental modeling contribution, but the leakage risk and inadequately controlled evidence currently prevent acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: lesion-level findings generation from whole-body PET/CT. PETARSeg-11K could be a valuable resource because it combines PET, CT, lesion masks, and textual descriptions at a scale not represented by the cited public datasets.

The focal-crop design is well motivated by the observation that lesions occupy less than 0.1% of a volume on average. Combining global context with a high-resolution lesion view is simple, relevant, and potentially useful beyond PET.

PETAR-4B reports substantial improvements over the evaluated fine-tuned baselines, including GREEN increasing from 0.071 for fine-tuned M3D-RAD to 0.257 and CIDEr from 0.132 to 0.457. The component ablations indicate that focal prompting is chiefly responsible for these gains.

The evaluation is broader than a purely metric-based study: it includes several 2D and 3D baselines, eight automated metrics, component ablations, an external AutoPET experiment, and ratings from five nuclear-medicine physicians.

The manuscript is generally understandable, and its figures communicate the intended mask-guided task and architecture effectively. weaknesses: A consequential evaluation risk is that the data split is insufficiently specified. The manuscript reports a held-out set of 1,175 "samples," but does not state that splitting occurs by patient or even by exam. Because an exam can contribute multiple lesion descriptions, lesion-level random splitting could place the same PET/CT volume and closely related report text in both training and test sets, substantially inflating every reported result.

The dataset is produced largely through LLM extraction and automatic SUV-guided thresholding, yet the paper does not directly validate the resulting 11,356 text-mask pairs. The cited 98% contour-location accuracy comes from prior work and does not establish mask quality, attribute-extraction accuracy, text-mask correspondence, or failure rates for this released collection. There is also no analysis by tracer, lesion size, anatomy, or extraction confidence.

The claimed clinical utility is weakened by removing all numeric values from the physician study specifically because the model hallucinates them. SUVmax and lesion dimensions are central PET findings. The assertion that they can be replaced by direct measurements describes an untested future pipeline, not the evaluated model. Consequently, the reader study excludes a known, clinically important failure mode while the conclusion describes the outputs as clinically useful.

The human-study reporting is inadequate for strong clinical conclusions. It is unclear whether every physician assessed every case, how ratings were aggregated, and what the effective sample size was. No inter-reader agreement, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or reader-level results are given. Counting 54 ties together with 15 model preferences to claim the model was "preferred, or considered equal" in about 60% of cases is also less informative than the criterion scores, on which human reports are consistently better.

The external evaluation contains only 32 manually curated AutoPET cases, has no reference reports or human-report comparator, and reports only mean physician scores. This is too small and selectively constructed to support the claim of consistent out-of-distribution performance, particularly given the single-site, predominantly FDG training cohort.

The ablation evidence contradicts parts of the interpretation. Focal prompting produces nearly all of the gain in GREEN (0.071 to 0.226), whereas adding the mask alone yields only 0.088 and CT alone reduces GREEN to 0.060. With focal prompting, adding CT markedly reduces RaTEScore from 0.698 to 0.587. Without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, the claims that each component improves all metrics and that CT clearly enhances factual or anatomical quality are not supported.

Baseline comparisons do not fully isolate the proposed architectural contribution. Mask-agnostic models are disadvantaged on a task where the target lesion is explicitly supplied to PETAR, while comparable baselines that receive the same mask-derived focal crop are absent. The automatic targets are also standardized by an LLM, so large overlap-metric gains may partly reflect learning a templated reporting style; direct attribute-level evaluation of anatomy, laterality, uptake interpretation, and hallucination is missing.

Reproducibility is limited by absent split identifiers and incomplete preprocessing, crop-size/resizing, inference, decoding, and random-seed details. There is also an internal inconsistency: the main paper states that all stages were trained for 10 epochs, whereas supplementary Table 9 lists 5 epochs; "full finetuning" is not reconciled with the stated LoRA training. No dataset URL, license, code release, or model checkpoint information is provided.

Overall, the dataset and focal-prompt idea are worthwhile, but uncertainty about train-test independence, insufficient validation of automatically constructed supervision, and a reader study that suppresses a known hallucination mode materially undermine the central empirical and clinical claims. These concerns currently outweigh the reported gains, leading to a weak-reject recommendation rather than a categorical rejection.

strengths: PETARSeg-11K addresses an important and underexplored problem: lesion-level grounding of free-text findings in whole-body 3D PET/CT. Its 11,356 descriptions from 5,126 exams, multiple tracers, paired volumes, and lesion masks could be a valuable community resource.

The focal-prompt design is technically sensible for lesions occupying less than 0.1% of a volume. PETAR-4B consistently outperforms the strongest fine-tuned baseline across all reported metrics, including GREEN (0.257 versus 0.086 for the best 2D baseline and 0.071 for M3D-RAD) and CIDEr (0.457 versus 0.132).
The evaluation is unusually broad for this task, covering 2D and 3D VLMs, conventional and clinically oriented text metrics, component ablations, qualitative examples, and an external AutoPET cohort.

The physician study is a major strength: five board-certified nuclear-medicine physicians assess anatomy, interpretation, and utility. PETAR obtains mean scores of 3.7–3.9 internally and 3.8–4.0 externally, and its outputs are preferred or tied with human findings in 69/116 internal cases.

The manuscript is generally clear and clinically motivated. It appropriately identifies mask acquisition as a deployment limitation and provides useful metric-versus-expert correlation results, with GREEN showing the strongest reported association (Spearman rho=0.592).
weaknesses: The ablations do not fully support the claimed importance of mask conditioning and CT fusion. Without focal prompting, adding the mask or CT decreases most metrics; with focal prompting, the mask gives negligible or mixed changes, and adding CT reduces RaTEScore from 0.700 to 0.613. Most of the gain comes from the focal crop. Moreover, the meaning of a focal-prompt ablation marked as not using a mask is unclear because the mask is required to locate the crop. These results warrant a more restrained architectural claim.

The data split is insufficiently specified. The paper gives only a held-out set of 1,175 samples and does not state train/validation sizes or whether separation is enforced at the patient level. Because multiple lesions and potentially multiple exams can belong to one patient, leakage across splits is a consequential possibility.

Baseline comparability is difficult to assess. Only selected baselines are fine-tuned, their optimization details are not reported, and the selection of the three slices supplied to 2D models is ambiguous. It is also unclear whether competing mask-aware models receive an equally high-resolution lesion-centered representation, so part of the advantage may arise from input presentation rather than the proposed fusion mechanism.

The human study omits important reliability and statistical details: whether every case was rated by every physician, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and reader-level analyses. The external set contains only 32 manually curated cases without reference reports, which provides encouraging but limited evidence for distributional generalization.

Numerical content such as SUV and lesion size is acknowledged to be hallucinated, then removed from the physician evaluation. These measurements are central to PET reporting, and saying they can be replaced from masks does not evaluate the proposed end-to-end output as presented. Reported clinical utility therefore reflects a restricted task and may be optimistic.

Dataset quality evidence is incomplete. Masks are automatically produced from report-derived SUV and slice cues, while the cited 98% location accuracy lacks the audited sample size and does not establish contour quality or text-mask correspondence across this dataset. No audit is reported for the Qwen-generated structured fields, tracer-specific subsets, or failure cases.

Reproducibility is limited by missing crop-size and resizing rules, patch/token dimensions, intensity normalization, decoding settings, seeds, per-stage schedules, and baseline configurations. There is also an apparent inconsistency between 10 training epochs in the main paper and 5 epochs in Supplementary Table 9, and no concrete dataset/code release link or licensing information is provided.
